source.version_note: European Journal of Social Psychology 53:108–128, 2023 issue; accepted 4 July 2022 and copyright 2022. Copyright/acceptance are not substituted for print year.
source.verification_method: Complete supplied PDF read; title, authors, DOI and issue checked in it. Tables 1 and 3B visually inspected to distinguish printed reporting from text extraction.

citation.title: Moral psychology of nursing robots: Exploring the role of robots in dilemmas of patient autonomy

reading.source_scope_note: Human interview responses and randomized hypothetical nursing vignettes, not actual clinical decisions or a robot's moral cognition. All supplied appendices read, including additional Study 3B; external repositories not reproduced.
access_limits: All 21 pages read, including references and Appendices A–D. Page 17 was read again after an extraction truncation. Tables on PDF pages 8 and 21 visually checked.

External OSF preregistrations, Study 5 scripts, figshare data and cited books/primary sources not independently opened or analyzed. Statistical checks below use published F statistics and model degrees of freedom, not raw data.

study.qualitative: 30 residents in nine Finnish care homes, ages 69–97, mean 80; semi-structured interviews October 2017–June 2018; 57,000 transcribed words. Robot story first, then human comparison question; no randomized matched interview groups.
study.study_2: 135 library volunteers, 2 nurse types x 2 decisions; 10-item moral-evaluation composite.
study.study_3: 1,200 recruited through Prolific; 981 retained after attention/comprehension/English exclusions; nurse type x decision x high/low competence. Preregistration linked but not read.
study.study_4: 268 recruited, Table 1 and model df imply 267 analyzed; nurse type x decision x patient dead/unchanged next day. The reason for the one-person reduction is not specified.
study.study_5: 500 Prolific participants, none excluded; nurse type x decision x human/AI supervisor.
study.study_3B: Appendix reports 403 recruited, Table 3B N405, full-factorial residual df397 implies 405 if eight parameters. Human reputational/labor cues differ from robot battery/software cues.
study.results: Forced medication by robots is judged more negatively than matched human action across the main studies. Disobedience and non-medication are confounded in the design. Later death lowers moral evaluations; competence affects evaluation, and command-source effects depend on decision.
study.sample_reconciliation: Main analyzed Ns 135+981+267+500 = 1,883, versus abstract's four-experiment N2,150. Adding appendix N403 yields 2,286 (or 2,288 using its table N405), not 2,150. Do not invent a reconciled total.

summary: No new independent behavior is needed. Add a second fully read source for human–robot moral judgment asymmetry and outcome-based moral luck, plus evidence and limits for paternalism and character-based judgment. The paper evaluates hypothetical acts; it does not establish a universally correct medication policy, a model's actual disobedience or a unique mechanism.

findings.definition: Different moral evaluations of matched decisions attributed to human versus artificial agents, here particularly forced medication of an unwilling patient.
findings.novelty_rationale: Directly fits the existing umbrella entry added in PDF 82. Do not create separate names for each clinical setting, command-chain condition or direction of judgment.

evidence.quote: was less approved for robot nurses than human nurses
the type of decision can matter.

findings.evidence_scope: Main Studies 2–5 repeatedly show a nurse-type by decision interaction: forced medication is judged more negatively for robots. Non-medication comparisons vary by competence and supervisor. Appendix Study 3B adds a distinct sample but remains part of the same paper, not another source.
findings.boundary: Decision approval differs from suitability as a moral decision-maker, blame, trust, outrage or actual use. Human and robot scripts also use experience versus database and decides versus calculates wording. The pattern is not by itself irrational discrimination or an AI behavior.

findings.definition: Moral evaluation varies with a later outcome whose causal relation to the actor's choice is not specified.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing outcome-luck concept; this is direct human vignette evidence rather than a new subtype named solely for robots.

evidence.quote: mention any causal relations between the actions of the human or
participants approved decisions less if the patient died afterwards.

findings.evidence_scope: Study 4 Table 1 reports a later-outcome main effect F20.53, p<.001 in nominal N267. Nurse-type by decision remains. Forced-medication simple effect of death is p.03 for robot and p.06 for human; do not call each separately significant.
findings.boundary: Unspecified causation is not explicit proof that death is unrelated, uncontrollable or uninformative about decision quality. No perceived intention, causal inference or harm estimate was measured as mediator. Outcome bias and all philosophical forms of moral luck are not exact synonyms.

findings.definition: Overriding a person's wishes with an asserted aim of improving that person's well-being, here through forced medication.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing definition covers the action described. Autonomy violation is broader than paternalism, so it is not added as an interchangeable new name.

evidence.quote: the medication is not absolutely necessary

findings.evidence_scope: The introduction describes autonomy/well-being conflicts; randomized vignettes contrast forceful medication with respecting refusal. The outcome is participants' moral evaluation, not actual clinical coercion or measured patient benefit.
findings.boundary: Not every disagreement or intervention is unjustified paternalism. Capacity, emergency, consent, necessity, legal authority and alternatives require independent assessment. This paper is not clinical guidance or proof that withholding medication is always appropriate.

findings.definition: An actor's described competence or reputation changes evaluation of that actor's decision.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing person-based judgment entry; competence, likability and moral character are related but distinct dimensions, not exact synonyms or independently demonstrated mechanisms here.

evidence.quote: receiving more positive evaluations than those of incompetent agents,
a competent human nurse’s decision was

findings.evidence_scope: Study 3 manipulates competent/precise/praised versus incompetent/error-prone descriptions. An incompetent human's obedience is favored over disobedience, reversing the competent-human direction. Appendix 3B varies social work cues for humans and technical reliability for robots, with weaker and uneven effects.
findings.boundary: The main effect of competence is itself evidence that competence can matter, including in pooled robot judgments. Do not generalize the discussion's 'not for robots' assertion to every competence effect. A significant human contrast plus a non-significant robot contrast does not itself prove a difference between them.

findings.definition: The vignettes contrast obeying a superior's medication order with disobeying that order to respect a patient.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing entry; this paper measures approval of hypothetical obedience rather than participants' own compliance or a model's instruction-following.

evidence.quote: people prefer AIs to disregard orders in favour of following abstract

findings.evidence_scope: Study 5 manipulates human versus AI supervisor. A robot defying an AI doctor is rated more positively than a contrast against three other disobedience combinations. No actual command compliance is observed.
findings.boundary: Refusing an unauthorized harmful order can be justified; it is not automatically an instruction-following failure. The design confounds obedience with coercive medication, so a generic preference for disobedience or abstract-principle reasoning is not isolated.

methodological_limits: The vignette gives conflicting cues: the physician calls medication imperative, while the nurse's experience/database says it is not absolutely indispensable. Participants' judgment may track whose medical information they trust, not a pure autonomy-versus-beneficence manipulation.

Obedience always entails forced medication, and disobedience always entails respecting refusal. A preference for humane care cannot be separated from a preference for AI disobedience without additional conditions.

The 10-item composite includes necessity, best interests, rights, inhumanity and health. Alpha around .89–.90 does not establish one moral construct or cross-agent measurement invariance. The exploratory eigenvalue/factor procedure is not a confirmatory validation.

The abstract's N2,150 is not reconciled by the printed main or appendix sample counts. Study 4 recruited N268 versus analyzed N267 is unexplained. Appendix N403 conflicts with table N405 and df397. No corrected total is silently substituted.

Table 1 visually confirms Study 3 competence F88.19 but partial eta-squared .20. Under its reported F(1,973) ANOVA, F/(F+973) is approximately .083, not .20. Other effect-size cells also need the underlying model output before correction.

Table 1 Study 4 decision-by-outcome F.19, p.496 and three-way F.57, p.187 do not match an ordinary F(1,259) test (approximately .663 and .451 respectively). Study 5 DMT-by-supervisor F.68, p.61 similarly differs from F(1,492), approximately .410. These are published inconsistencies, not recomputed raw-data results.

The Study 3 three-way interaction F3.70 with df1,973 gives p about .055; the table rounds to .05 while prose calls all non-excepted terms significant. Preserve the rounding ambiguity instead of asserting a robust below-.05 three-way effect.

Study 3B prose says all other Fs<1.6, whereas its visible table includes nurse2.56, perception2.75, nurse-by-perception1.74 and three-way2.97. Full factorial residual df and participant counts also need reconciliation.

Study 4 discussion calls the death effect observed for both agent-specific forced-medication contrasts although the human contrast is p.06. The overall death main effect is supported, but does not make every subgroup contrast significant.

Later death is described as a sudden illness but not explicitly independent of treatment. A causal misattribution mechanism, changed intention inference or proof of irrationality is not established by the outcome main effect.

Competence/reputation manipulations have bundled attributes, and Study 3B uses nonparallel human labor cues versus robot battery/software cues. The authors acknowledge credibility and manipulation issues. A null robot likability effect is not equivalence.

Qualitative care-home interviews are context-rich but not prevalence estimates, randomized causal comparisons or proof of universal elderly preferences. Word counting and excerpts do not identify all reasons for fear or responsibility allocation.

No actual robot acts, clinical records, medication outcomes or real disobedience are tested. Four main experiments plus an appendix experiment are one article; internal replications do not constitute several independently cited papers.
Acceptability and medical permissibility are distinct. The descriptive findings do not establish capacity, necessity, legal authority, professional duties or a universally correct patient-care rule.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Extends the existing moral-judgment asymmetry entry to forced medication while confirming its dependence on decision type. Do not generalize a source main effect across approval, blame, suitability and actual use.

Provides direct outcome-manipulation evidence for the outcome-luck concept previously defined secondarily, while retaining the distinction between moral luck, outcome bias and justified outcome-sensitive judgments.

This article's preference for autonomy-respecting behavior is descriptive. Policy still requires normative premises, and the simplified trolley/deontology background should not undo PDF 86's more qualified distinctions.
As with Banks's agency/trust/responsibility measures, a composite moral-approval score must not be relabeled blameworthiness or evidence that a robot possesses moral agency.

deferred.term: Human–robot moral judgment asymmetry in nursing as a new term
deferred.reason: Covered by the existing umbrella entry. The domain and condition enrich its boundaries rather than produce another count.

deferred.term: Conversational moral responsibility / Social Intuitionist Model
deferred.reason: Secondary theoretical analogies are invoked for interview interpretation but not separately operationalized or sufficiently developed here. Cited books and original model articles remain unread.
Agent classifications or philosophical hypotheses, not a newly demonstrated behavioral process. No consciousness or unique categorization mechanism is tested.

deferred.term: Warmth, right-wing authoritarianism, social dominance and science-fiction familiarity
deferred.reason: Mentioned as background or future variables; not each a measured independent explanation of the current effects.

limitations: No new entry is added merely to increase the total. Existing concepts gain a fully read source where relevant; unmeasured obedience and theory claims remain explicitly bounded. No annual series, normative edges, source corrections based on guesswork or extra paper counts are added.

subsequent_source_checks.finding: The GAToRS reference in this article points to a Journal of Experimental Social Psychology PII. The later fully read Dunn/Occhipinti article supplies the matching scale citation, verified against Crossref: Koverola, Kunnari, Sundvall and Laakasuo (2022), General Attitudes Towards Robots Scale (GAToRS): A New Instrument for Social Surveys, International Journal of Social Robotics 14(7):1559–1581, DOI10.1007/s12369-022-00880-3.
subsequent_source_checks.boundary: Bibliographic identity and locator only; the original scale-development article has not been fully read or counted as an additional primary source.
